review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The revision is right. On the images of p. 459 (last lines) and p. 460, the paper applies the fibre bound for m^{-1}(ϖ^λ) to 'the preimage of X^H_≤λ((Nm b)σ_E)'. Read literally, the inference 'dim of preimage ≤ dim X_≤λ + (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ)' is not justified. Points of X_≤λ that lie in a smaller stratum X_λ' (λ' < λ) have fibres of dimension up to (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ'), which can exceed (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ). For λ = |μ•| the literal argument would bound the whole of X_≤μ• by dim X_≤|μ•| + 0. But the displayed bound is itself true, and the conclusion follows by the obvious stratified reading. Assume (3.1.3) for H. For each λ' ≤ |μ•|, the preimage of the exact stratum X_λ' has dimension ≤ (ρ_H, λ' − ν_{Nm b}) − ½def_H(Nm b) + (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ') = (ρ_H, |μ•| − ν_{Nm b}) − ½def_H(Nm b). This number does not depend on λ'. X_≤μ• is the finite union of these preimages, so the upper bound holds, and Lemma 3.7 converts it to (ρ_G, μ − ν_b) − ½def_G(b). Equality: for λ' < |μ•| we have (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ') ≥ 1, since |μ•| − λ' is a nonzero sum of positive coroots. So by (3.1.3) for H every closed stratum X_≤λ' has strictly smaller dimension than X_≤|μ•| (when the latter is nonempty). Hence the open stratum X_|μ•| is nonempty and of full dimension. Over it m is bijective (the fibre over ϖ^{|μ•|} is a point), which gives equality. So replacing '≤λ' by the exact stratum 'λ' (the text says 'for λ' and uses the fibre over ϖ^λ) makes the proof correct as written. The meaning is clear and nothing downstream changes, so the right classification is misprint/nothing, not error/'the proof'. I checked that arXiv v3 has the same wording. arXiv v2 (PDF p. 36) writes 'dim X^H_≤μ•(Nm(b)) = max_λ dim X^H_≤λ(Nm b) + (ρ_H, |μ•| − λ)', with the same looseness. Nonemptiness is tacit here, as in (3.1.3) throughout (ledger issue E19).

review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation is verbatim on the p. 480 image, and v2 and v3 have the same. The revised argument is correct, and it strengthens the ledger's. Let X = (P^1_k)^{p^-∞} with model ε: X -> P^1, and let F: P^1 -> P^1, [x:y] ↦ [x^p:y^p], be the k-linear relative Frobenius (P^1 is defined over F_p). Its perfection φ is a k-automorphism of X, the perfection of a universal homeomorphism (cf. Cor. A.16), with ε∘φ = F∘ε. So (P^1, F∘ε) is another model in the paper's sense (p. 471). F is finite flat of degree p and F^*O(1) = O(p) (cf. Remark A.24), so F^* acts by p on H^2(P^1_k̄, Q̄_ℓ(1)), and the standard trace satisfies Tr∘F^* = p·Tr. So the paper's claim that model morphisms f^* are 'compatible with c_{X'} and c_{X''}' fails already for model comparisons, and the two models give values of c_X that differ by p. There is no way to repair this intrinsically. φ^* acts by p on the line H^2_c(X_k̄, Q̄_ℓ(1)), so an isomorphism c_X invariant under k-automorphisms of X would force c_X = p·c_X. The 'alternative' construction via Pic((P^1)^{p^-∞}) = Z[1/p] has the same ambiguity, because the generator is determined only up to p^Z (Remark A.24). In general, comparison maps between models are finite universal homeomorphisms of p-power degree, so c_X, [X] and cl(Z) are defined only up to factors in p^Z. The ledger's 'normalization proof remains open' should therefore become 'no model-independent normalization exists'. review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The page image (p. 488) prints 'g̃ := X̃Ã^{−1} = p^{−2}X̃Ã^* ∈ LGL_2'. The decomposition sought is X = Ag: see the definition of W on p. 487, the multiplication 'by X^* on the left and g^{−1} on the right' that gives X^*A, and the conclusion 'then X = Ag'. With the printed order, X̃ = g̃Ã, which is the wrong side. The printed quantity is also not integral in general. Take A = (p −1; 0 p) (x = z = 0, y = 1, so x² = yz and det A = p²) and g = (1 0; 1 1). Then X = Ag = (p−1 −1; p p), with det X = p². Its Teichmüller digits are a_0 = −1, a_1 = 1, b_0 = −1, b_1 = 0, c_0 = 0, c_1 = 1, d_0 = 0, d_1 = 1, so a_1d_1 − b_1c_1 = 1 and X ∈ W̃. (B.3.3) returns x = 0, y = 1, z = 0, which is this A. But XA^* = (p²−p −1; p² p²+p), so XA^{−1} has entry −1/p². With the order corrected, the proof works. For p > 2, (B.3.2) is equivalent to X^*A ≡ 0 mod p²: the p^0 terms cancel exactly as Teichmüller sums, e.g. [d_0x] + [−b_0z] = 0 when d_0x = b_0z, and the p^1 terms give the second equation. For 2×2 matrices, adj(X^*A) = A^*X, so A^*X ≡ 0 mod p². Hence p^{−2}Ã^*X̃ is integral, with determinant det X̃/p² ∈ W(R)^*. Both expressions in the display must be changed.

review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The revision is right on each point I checked. (1) Locator: the sentence 'Proofs are generally omitted in this section.' is on p. 482 (PDF p. 80), in the opening paragraph of Appendix B, not on p. 484. (2) The following have no proof at all: Prop. B.1, Lemma B.9, and the final paragraph of B.3 ('one can also verify Conjecture I in this case'). The following have only hints or sketches: Prop. B.2 (one sentence), Lemma B.4 ('We give a hint of the proof'), Lemma B.7 and Prop. B.8 ('Details are left to readers'). The unnumbered assertions are unproved: on p. 485, that conditions (3)–(4) cut out M_{N,h} as an irreducible component; on p. 486, that \mathring M_{N,h} ≃ Gr′_N; and in Remark B.6. (3) The existing entry is wrong to list Lemmas B.10–B.11 as unproved, and I rechecked their proofs. (B.3.1) is correct: for 2×2 matrices, X_1X_0^* + X_0X_1^* = tr(X_1X_0^*)·I. In (B.3.3), when a_1d_1 − b_1c_1 is a unit, the second equation of (B.3.2) forces m = X_1X_0^*/(b_1c_1 − a_1d_1). This m is traceless because 2·tr(X_1X_0^*) = 0 and p > 2, has det m = det X_0/det X_1 = 0, and satisfies X_0^*m = 0 because X_0^*X_1X_0^* = −det(X_0)X_1^* = 0. The step W = W̃G and the uniqueness of A are sound, since A ∈ W̃ with A_1 = A_2(g_2g_1^{−1}). The remaining 'argument as in Lemma 1.10' also goes through. For (E,β,ε̄) in V, the image X = Ag lies in W. Transporting along the unique α with β∘α = Ã gives (E_0, Ã, h) with Ah = X. That point is the image of (A, h), so the map is surjective. It is injective because A is unique and β∘α = β forces α = id. The only defects in these proofs are E32 and E33. (4) Prop. B.2's sentence tacitly needs \tilde L_det to be trivial on the fibres of π. That follows from base-point-freeness together with the second part of Prop. B.1 (degree 0 on fibre curves, itself unproved). The fibres are connected (Lemma 1.18), and π_*O = O (Lemma A.21). (5) The Lemma B.4 hint is sound: the stabilizer of diag(p^{m_i}) has dimension nΣm_i = nN, and so does that of every double-coset translate. Hence dim V_{N,h} = N(n−1) + n²h − nN = n²h − N. The main theorems do not use Appendix B. §§0–3 cite it only in remarks, footnote 5 and the introduction. So the gap affects only the appendix's own stated results. Footnote 21 records that Bhatt–Scholze proved Conjectures I–II.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 407: "Let G be a reductive group over O, the ring of integers of a p-adic field F, and let Gr_G denote its affine Grassmannian. ... As in the equal characteristic situation, this is a semisimple monoidal category"; then Theorem 0.3 (p. 408) with no hypothesis on k.
sourceIssues.correction: In §0.2 (p. 407) and Theorem 0.3 (p. 408), assume that the residue field k over which Gr_G is formed is algebraically closed (and that G is connected reductive), as in §2, p. 429. Equivalently, work with Gr_G ⊗_k k̄.
sourceIssues.reason: In the introduction k is the residue field of F (§0.1.1, p. 404; §0.1.3, p. 405), and for a p-adic field it is finite. Over a finite k the semisimplicity claim and Theorem 0.3 fail. For G = G_m, Gr_G is the discrete set X_• = Z, and P_{L+G}(Gr_G) is the direct sum over Z of the categories of continuous Q̄_ℓ-representations of Gal(k̄/k). That category is not semisimple (Frobenius can act by a unipotent Jordan block), and H* does not give an equivalence onto Rep(Ĝ_m) = Z-graded vector spaces. The body proves the theorem only for algebraically closed k (§2, p. 429), and item T07 correctly includes that hypothesis. Case for the defence: introductions are informal, geometric Satake is conventionally stated over an algebraically closed field, §0.3 sets k = F̄_p two pages later, and the body states the hypothesis explicitly. That is why I class it as a misprint affecting nothing.

review.reason: The quotations match the images of pp. 407–408. The setting is 'Let G be a reductive group over O, the ring of integers of a p-adic field F, and let Gr_G denote its affine Grassmannian ... this is a semisimple monoidal category', and Theorem 0.3 imposes no condition on k. Gr_G lives over k, which §0.1.1 (p. 404) defines as the residue field of the local field F; for a p-adic field k is finite. Even §0.5 (p. 411) fixes only 'a perfect field k'. The hypothesis first appears in §2 (p. 429): 'we assume that k is algebraically closed and that G is a connected reductive group scheme over O in this section'. So the missing hypothesis is not a convention stated elsewhere. For finite k both claims fail, for every G. The base point Gr_0 = L^+G/L^+G ≅ Spec k is a closed L^+G-orbit on which the connected group L^+G acts trivially. L^+G-equivariant perverse sheaves supported there are the continuous finite-dimensional Q̄_ℓ-representations of Gal(k̄/k). That category is not semisimple: Frobenius can act by the unipotent Jordan block [[1,1],[0,1]], which extends continuously to Ẑ → GL_2(Z_ℓ). Moreover, on these sheaves H* only forgets the Galois action. It is not full, since two different Frobenius characters are non-isomorphic sheaves with isomorphic H* = Q̄_ℓ, so H* does not factor through an equivalence onto Rep(Ĝ). The first reading's G_m example is a special case. For a non-split G over finite k, 'Ĝ' is also not the right target. Case for the defence, which I accept for the classification: the introduction is informal, §0.3 takes k = F̄_p on p. 409, geometric Satake is conventionally stated over an algebraically closed field, and the body theorem (§2) carries the hypothesis. The ledger item T07 already includes it. Misprint, affects nothing.

sourceIssues.reason: Without simplicity the claim is false. Take G = PGL_2 × PGL_3 over O, which is adjoint. If b_i is superbasic in PGL_i (for example the class with Kottwitz invariant 1), then b = (b_1, b_2) is superbasic in G. A proper F-Levi of G has the form M_1 × M_2 with some M_i proper, and b_i does not meet a proper Levi of PGL_i. Yet G is neither PGL_n nor Res_{E/F} PGL_n. The proof on p. 457 first reduces to simple adjoint G, so nothing downstream is affected.

review.reason: The quotation matches the image of p. 410, and p. 456 repeats the sentence with G_F. The literal claim is false. Take G = PGL_2 × PGL_3 over O, which is unramified and adjoint. Parabolic subgroups, and hence Levi subgroups over F, of a product are products M_1 × M_2 of Levis of the factors, and σ-conjugacy is taken componentwise. Let b_i be superbasic in PGL_i, for example the basic class with Kottwitz invariant 1 in Z/i. If some σ-conjugate of b = (b_1, b_2) lay in a proper M_1 × M_2, then some M_i would be proper and b_i would meet it, a contradiction. So b is superbasic. Yet G_F is neither PGL_n nor Res_{E/F} PGL_n, being neither simple nor a restriction of scalars of PGL_n from a field. The same argument shows that for adjoint G, superbasic classes exist exactly when every F-simple factor is Res_{E_i/F} PGL_{n_i}. The paper's own proof (p. 457) says 'one can assume that G = G_ad is simple of adjoint type. Then it follows from [GHKR06], [CKV15] that superbasic b exists only when G_F = Res_{E/F} PGL_n'. The intended hypothesis is therefore clear, and the argument that is actually run is correct. The slip is confined to the paraphrases on pp. 410 and 456.

Take 𝒪 = W(k), h = 1 and 𝒳 = 𝔸^1: the formula gives R ↦ W(R)/pW(R) = W(R)/VFW(R). Here V[t] ∉ VFW(k[t]), since that would need t to be a p-th power, but V[t] becomes 0 after the fpqc cover k[t] → k[t^{1/p}]. So this functor is not even fpqc-separated, let alone a finite-type scheme. The intended functor is Greenberg's, as the citation says. p. 419 confirms this: it writes L_p^hM_n = 𝔸^{n²h} and L_p^h𝔸^1 = 𝔸^h, which hold for W_h(R) and fail for W(R)/p^h. So this is a notational slip whose meaning is clear, and nothing downstream is affected. The proposed correction needs fixing, however. W_m(R) ⊗_{W_m(k)} 𝒪/ϖ^h with merely em ≥ h is not well defined: for e = 1, h = 1, m = 2 it gives W_2(R)/pW_2(R) ≠ R. Even with m = ⌈h/e⌉ it is wrong when e ∤ h. For 𝒪 = W(k)[√p] and h = 3 it contains W_2(R)/pW_2(R) ≅ R × R/R^p (as sets) as a summand, which is not representable, whereas Greenberg's functor is.

sourceIssues.printed: In other words, étale locally on R a trivialization ε as in the definition of L′G always exists. Claim (a) follows. … Then it follows that Gr_G = Gr′_G.
sourceIssues.correction: Add that every fpqc L^+G-torsor P over an affine perfect Spec R is étale-locally trivial. Its push-out to L^hG, the perfection of the smooth group L_p^hG and hence pfp, is étale-locally trivial by Corollary A.27. The kernels of L^{h+1}G → L^hG are perfections of vector groups, whose torsors over affine perfect schemes are trivial. So a section of the push-out lifts step by step, and P = lim_h P ×^{L^+G} L^hG has a section. Hence the fpqc quotient [LG/L^+G] equals the étale quotient, which is Gr′_G by (a), (b) and étale descent along W_𝒪(R) → W_𝒪(R′). Alternatively, prove directly that Gr′_G is an fpqc sheaf: use descent on each W_{𝒪,n}(R), p-adic limits for the torsor, and bounded denominators for β. For GL_n this is Kreidl's theorem, cited in footnote 4.
sourceIssues.reason: Gr_G is defined (§1.1.2, §A.1.4) as the quotient in the fpqc topology: its R-points are pairs (P, φ) with P an fpqc L^+G-torsor. The proof only shows that ε exists étale-locally for (𝓔, β) ∈ Gr′_G. That identifies Gr′_G with the étale sheafification of the presheaf quotient LG/L^+G. Passing to Gr_G needs either that Gr′_G is an fpqc sheaf, i.e. fpqc descent of G-torsors on W_𝒪(R) with trivializations, which is not addressed, or that fpqc L^+G-torsors are étale-locally trivial. Corollary A.27 covers only pfp groups, and L^+G is not pfp. Both facts are true, so the lemma holds, but the argument as written is incomplete. Lemma 1.9 ('By the same proof of Lemma 1.3') and the moduli description of Gr̄_{N,h} inherit the omission.

review.reason: The quoted sentences are on p. 414, but in the opposite order: 'Then it follows that Gr_G = Gr′_G.' comes right after claims (a) and (b) and before 'Let 𝓔 be a G-torsor … In other words, étale locally … Claim (a) follows.' The substance is confirmed. Gr_G = [LG/L^+G] is the quotient in the fpqc topology on perfect k-algebras (§1.1.2, §§A.1.3–A.1.4), and its points are pairs (P, φ) with P an fpqc L^+G-torsor. The proof shows only that, for (𝓔, β) ∈ Gr′_G, a trivialization ε exists étale locally, and that LG ≅ L′G. From this, Gr_G = Gr′_G follows only if one of two facts holds. Either Gr′_G is an fpqc sheaf, in which case LG → Gr′_G is an L^+G-torsor in Sp^pf and Gr′_G is the quotient. Or every fpqc L^+G-torsor is étale-locally trivial. Neither is proved or cited. Corollary A.27 needs a pfp group, and L^+G is not pfp. The composite H^k_{S̄^-_λ}(A) → H^k(A) → H^k(S̄_{λ′},A) is the isomorphism of (2.2.10) (hyperbolic localization at ϖ^λ) for λ′ = λ. It is zero for λ′ ≠ λ of the same degree, since a nonempty closed G_m-stable S̄^-_λ ∩ S̄_{λ′} contains some ϖ^η with λ ≤ η ≤ λ′. Hence H^k(A) = ⊕_{(2ρ,λ)=k} Im(H^k_{S̄^-_λ}(A) → H^k(A)), which gives H^* ≅ ⊕_λ H^*_c(S_λ,−).

So the printed Fil′_{<λ} vanishes in degree (2ρ,λ) and cannot split off the λ-piece. Morally it is ⊕_{λ′>λ}, which lies inside Fil_{≥λ} instead of complementing it. review.reason: The quotation matches p. 436. By Prop. 2.5, S^-_{<λ} := S̄^-_λ − S^-_λ = ∪_{λ′>λ} S^-_{λ′}. By (2.2.10) and Prop. 2.7, H^*_{S^-_{λ′}}(A) is concentrated in degree (2ρ,λ′), and (2ρ,λ′−λ) ∈ 2Z_{>0} for λ′ > λ. So the printed Fil′_{<λ} vanishes in degree (2ρ,λ), the only degree of the λ-piece. It consists of pieces λ′ > λ, which already lie in Fil_{≥λ}, so it cannot complement it. I verified the first reading's counterexample: GL_2, A = IC_{(1,0)} = Q̄_ℓ[1] on P^1, λ = (0,1). Here S_{<λ} ∩ P^1 = ∅, so Fil_{≥λ} = H^*(A). S^-_{<λ} ∩ P^1 = S^-_{(1,0)} ∩ P^1 = {ϖ^{(1,0)}}, and H^1_{pt}(A) → H^1(A) = H^2(P^1) is the (nonzero) point class. So Fil_{≥λ} ∩ Fil′_{<λ} ≠ 0 and the sum is not direct. The printed filtration is thus not complementary to Fil, and 'these two filtrations are complimentary by (2.2.10)' is a false step. Corollary 2.10 itself is correct by the argument of [MV07, Th. 3.6], which the proof cites, run with the images of H^*_{S̄^-_λ} instead of H^*_{S̄^-_λ − S^-_λ}. The same text is in v3.

sourceIssues.correction: Delete item (2), or state: Q_{1/2} is the parahoric of −θ/2, whose reductive quotient contains the SL_2 of the affine roots ±(θ^∨+1). It is maximal unless the simple factor containing θ is of type A_n with n ≥ 2.
sourceIssues.reason: Q_{1/2} is the parahoric of −θ/2 (v2: 'the point −μ/2 is a vertex'). The affine roots vanishing there are ±(θ^∨ + 1) and the roots orthogonal to θ. These have full rank only if the roots orthogonal to the highest root have rank r − 1, which fails in type A_n, n ≥ 2, where they have rank n − 2. For SL_3, θ = (1,0,−1) pairs to 1 or 2 with every positive root. So −θ/2 lies on the single wall θ^∨ + 1 = 0, inside an edge, and Q_{1/2} is properly contained in the parahorics of the edge's two vertices. Type A is covered by the paper: θ ∈ M (p. 439) and Lemma 2.11 includes it. The claim is not used in any proof.

review.reason: The quotation matches p. 437. Q_{1/2} is generated by T(O) and U_α(ϖ^{⌈⟨θ,α⟩/2⌉}O), i.e. it is the parahoric of the point x = −θ/2. The affine roots vanishing at x are ±(θ^∨+1) and the roots α with ⟨θ,α⟩ = 0. So x is a vertex (Q_{1/2} maximal) iff the roots orthogonal to the highest root θ^∨ have rank r − 1. That holds exactly when α_0 meets a single node of the extended Dynkin diagram, which fails in type A_n, n ≥ 2 (the roots orthogonal to e_1 − e_{n+1} form A_{n−2}). Concretely, for SL_3 and θ = (1,0,−1), every positive root pairs to 1 or 2 with θ. So x = (−1/2,0,1/2) lies only on the walls ±(e_1−e_3+1) and is interior to an edge. Q_{1/2} is then strictly contained in the parahoric of the vertex (−1/3,−1/3,2/3) of that edge. Type A is within the lemma's scope (M on p. 439 contains θ for SL_n and GL_n). arXiv v2 justified the claim by 'the point −μ/2 is a vertex', which is the false step. The claim is not used: Lemma 2.12(i) needs only the A_1 factor ±(θ^∨+1) of the reductive quotient. The use of R_{L̄Q_{1/2}} in Lemma 2.19 (p. 442) needs only W_{Q_{1/4}} ⊂ W_{Q_{1/2}} ⊂ W.

review.reason: The display and (2.2.13) on p. 439 match the quotation. By Lemma 2.12(ii), π^{-1}(Gr_0) is the whole section at infinity Σ_∞ = Q_0 ×^{Q_{1/4}} Q_{1/4}sQ_{3/4}/Q_{3/4} ≅ Ḡ/P̄_θ, and Gr_0 ⊂ S_0. The printed right side lies in φ^{-1}(Y), Y = ∪_{wθ<0} ŪwP̄/P̄, so it misses Σ_∞ over Ḡ/P̄ − Y (the cells with wθ > 0). The printed formula then contradicts (2.2.12). Write β = wθ. The cell dimension is #{α>0 : ⟨α,β⟩ > 0}, which equals ht θ + ht β − 1 for β > 0 and ht θ − ht(−β) for β < 0, and d = 2ht θ = dim Ḡ/P̄_θ + 1. With the printed (2.2.13), H^i_c(π^{-1}(S_0 ∩ Gr_{≤θ}), Q̄_ℓ[d]) = 0 for i > 0. But H^i(𝒞) = H^{i+d}(Ḡ/P̄_θ) ≠ 0 for i = 2ht β − 2 > 0 whenever some positive β ∈ Wθ has height ≥ 2 (e.g. β = θ, if ht θ ≥ 2). In degree 0 both sides have dimension |Δ_θ|, which forces H^0_c(S_0, IC_θ) = 0. SL_3 check: Ḡ/P̄_θ is the flag variety and 𝒞 = Q̄_ℓ[2] ⊕ Q̄_ℓ^2 ⊕ Q̄_ℓ[−2]. The printed (2.2.13) gives Q̄_ℓ[2] ⊕ Q̄_ℓ^2, which is impossible. With the missing piece added, the Ḡ/P̄ − Y term reproduces H^i(𝒞) for i ≥ 0 and the Y term reproduces it for i < 0. sourceIssues.correction: In Lemma 2.28 and in the Θ-diagram (p. 449), c_vect must denote the Koszul-signed commutativity of graded vector spaces, a⊗b → (-1)^{|a||b|} b⊗a. Only in Proposition 2.21 and Corollary 2.22 is c_vect the plain flip.
sourceIssues.reason: The right column of Lemma 2.28 uses θ^*(A_1⋆A_2) ≃ θ^*A_2⋆θ^*A_1, which comes from (θ×~θ)^*(A_1⊠~A_2) ≃ θ^*A_2⊠~θ^*A_1, i.e. from interchanging the factors of an external product. Under Künneth this interchange induces the Koszul-signed flip. There is also an internal check. By the Θ-diagram and Lemma 2.29, H^*(c') = c_vect, since the powers √−1^i·√−1^j/√−1^{i+j} cancel. If c_vect were the plain flip, then the Koszul change (2.4.4) (intended (−1)^{ε1ε2}, E15) would give H^*(c) = (−1)^{ε(A1)ε(A2)}·flip, contradicting Proposition 2.21 for two odd objects (e.g. G = PGL_2, A_1 = A_2 = IC_ω, whose cohomology sits in degrees ±1). With the Koszul flip, H^*(c) = (−1)^{ε1ε2}(−1)^{ij}·flip = flip, because H^j(A) = 0 unless j ≡ ε(A) mod 2 (Lemma 1.25 and the parity of IC stalks). In the paper's defence, the text calls (2.4.4) a 'Koszul sign change' and cites [BD] and [MV07], so the intended reading can be recovered. LY13 (published §3.3) use the non-Koszul flip only because all their objects are even (G simply connected). Read literally, Lemma 2.28 is false by the sign (−1)^{ij}. The same text is in v2 and v3.

review.reason: The quotations match the images of pp. 443 and 449. In Lemma 2.28 and the Θ-diagram, c_vect is not redefined, so it is literally the 'usual flip' of Proposition 2.21. I re-derived the sign. (1) Geometry: the right column of Lemma 2.28 comes from (θ x~ θ)^*(A1 ⊠~ A2) = θ^*A2 ⊠~ θ^*A1, where θ x~ θ sends (g1,g2) to (θ(g2), θ(g1)). This interchanges the factors, and under Künneth such an interchange acts by a x b → (-1)^{|a||b|} b x a. (2) Internal consistency: the Θ-diagram follows from Lemmas 2.27–2.28, and Lemma 2.29 gives Θ = √−1^j on H^j. On H^i(A1) ⊗ H^j(A2) the factors √−1^{i+j} cancel, so H^*(c') equals the c_vect of Lemma 2.28. If that c_vect were the plain flip, then c = c' would already satisfy Proposition 2.21, and the announced Koszul change (2.4.4) (E15) would destroy it for two odd objects. Example: G = PGL_2, A1 = A2 = IC_ω with Gr_ω = P^1, whose cohomology lies in degrees ±1; H^*(c) would be -flip. With the Koszul flip, H^j(A) = 0 unless j ≡ ε(A) mod 2 (Lemma 1.25 and parity vanishing), so H^*(c) = (-1)^{ε1 ε2}(-1)^{ij} flip = flip, as Proposition 2.21 requires. This is also the MV07 mechanism (§6, after Remark 6.2). LY13 (published §3.3) state that they use the unadjusted flip on Vec^gr, which is harmless there because G is simply connected and every object is even. So read literally, Lemma 2.28 is false by (-1)^{ij}, and the only consistent reading is the Koszul flip. The phrase 'Koszul sign change' signals this, so the meaning is recoverable (misprint, nothing). v2 and v3 have the same text.

Specializing along R_{Ḡ,ℓ} → Q̄_ℓ gives the lemma in all degrees.
sourceIssues.reason: The cohomology ring of a partial flag variety need not be generated in degree 2. Counterexample: G = GL_4 and μ = (1,1,0,0) (minuscule), for which Gr_μ = (Ḡ/P̄_μ)^{p^{−∞}} = Gr(2,4)^{p^{−∞}}. There H^2 is spanned by σ_1, H^4 is 2-dimensional (σ_2, σ_{1,1}) and σ_1² = σ_2 + σ_{1,1}, so H^4 is not spanned by products of degree-2 classes. The reduction as written therefore fails for such μ. LY13 (published Lemma 4.3) use only degrees ≤ 2, via IH^i ≅ H^i(Ω_λ) for i ≤ 2, so the claim is Zhu's own. Lemma 2.32 itself remains true, since the proof's own equivariant computation covers all degrees. The same claim is in v2 and v3.

review.reason: The claim is real. The quotation matches the image of p. 451, and v2 and v3 have the same sentence. The rational cohomology of a partial flag variety need not be generated in degree 2. Take G = GL_4 and μ = (1,1,0,0), which is minuscule. P_μ, generated by the U_α with <α,μ> <= 0, has Levi GL_2 x GL_2, so Gr_μ = Gr(2,4)^{p^{−∞}} (Corollary 1.24; dim = (2ρ,μ) = 4). The Betti numbers are 1,1,2,1,1. Since H^2 is one-dimensional, Sym^2 H^2 cannot span the two-dimensional H^4. So the stated reduction 'it is enough to prove Θ̊_μ = -1 on H^2' is invalid for such μ. The case is used: Lemma 2.32 is needed in all degrees for Gr_λ in the proof of Lemma 2.30 and in Remark 2.33 (minuscule μ). LY13 (published Lemma 4.3) use only degrees <= 2, so this claim is Zhu's own. The lemma remains true, and the repair is in the same proof. θ^* and γ are ring maps, R_{L_μ} = R_T^{W_L} is contained in R_T, and the diagram shows the equivariant map is induced by χ → -χ on the polynomial ring R_T, which is generated in degree 2. So it is (-1)^j in degree 2j, and it descends to H^*(Gr_μ) = Q̄_ℓ ⊗_{R_G} R_{L_μ}. Reclassify the reach: the proof as written makes a false assertion and an invalid reduction, so it affects the proof. No stated result is affected, and 'nothing' understates a genuinely false step.

review.reason: The quotation matches the image of p. 452, and v2 and v3 have the same text. Gr_λ is smooth of dimension d_λ = (2ρ,λ), and IC_μ is Verdier self-dual up to a Tate twist. So i_λ^! IC_μ = (i_λ^* IC_μ)^*[2d_λ] on stalks. For C_μ = IC_μ[s] this gives i^!C_μ = (i^*C_μ)^*[2d_λ + 2s]. With the intended s = -(2ρ,μ) (E16) this is (i^*C_μ)^*[2(2ρ,λ-μ)] = (i^*C_μ[2(2ρ,μ-λ)])^*. The printed formula has the shift inside the dual with the wrong sign. It is also wrong with the printed normalization s = +(2ρ,μ), which needs [2(2ρ,λ+μ)] against the printed [2(2ρ,μ-λ)]. Checks: SL_2, μ = α^∨, λ = 0, intended normalization: C_μ = Q̄_ℓ (rationally smooth cone), i^!_0 C_μ = Q̄_ℓ[-4], but the printed formula gives Q̄_ℓ[4]. λ = μ, printed normalization: i^!_μ C_μ = Q̄_ℓ[2(2ρ,μ)], but the printed formula gives Q̄_ℓ[-2(2ρ,μ)]. The argument uses only parity. The inverse dual of H^*Ψ on H^{2b}(i^!C) acts by (-1)^{b + (2ρ,μ-λ)} = (-1)^b, since μ - λ lies in the coroot lattice. So the conclusion gr Θ = (-1)^j on degree 2j stands.

sourceIssues.printed: The usual Kazhdan-Lusztig theory [KL79], [KL80] works in our situation. … On the other hand, in [LV12, §3], similar interpretations were given to the polynomials P^{σ,⋄}_{y,w}. Such interpretations in particular imply that P^{σ,⋄}_{dλ,dμ}(q) = Σ tr(H^{2j}_λΨ_μ | H^{2j}_λC_μ)q^j.
sourceIssues.correction: Prove, on the perfect Witt-vector affine flag variety and for ⋄ = Ad(ω)∘*, the Lusztig–Vogan trace realization of P^{σ,⋄}_{y,w} (the analogue of [LV12, §3] and [LY13, published (3.2), (3.5), §7.4 with (7.1)]), including the Kazhdan–Lusztig purity and parity input. Then show that the resulting stalk involution on H^{2j}_λ C_μ equals Zhu's Ψ_μ = (Cor. 2.26)∘N_μ, via an Iwahori-level analogue of Lemma 2.24 and Corollary 2.26 compatible with pullback along Fl → Gr.
sourceIssues.reason: [LV12, §3] proves the trace interpretation of P^σ_{y,w} only for finite Weyl groups (flag varieties over F̄_p). §7.1–7.2 of LV12 assert, without proof, that it extends to affine Weyl groups over k((ε)) and to twisted ⋄. LY13 (published §3.1) call their affine version 'an elaboration of this remark'. Zhu needs it for the mixed-characteristic affine flag variety and the ⋄-twisted parahoric setting, with his own Ψ_μ built from Gr^op and Corollary 2.26, and he asserts it in one sentence. This formula is the only link between Theorem 2.35 and Lemma 2.34, and through Lemmas 2.30 and 2.29 it carries Proposition 2.21 and Theorem 0.3. In the paper's defence, the LV argument is formal: it uses the sheaf-function dictionary, purity and parity vanishing, and rank-one P^1-computations. All of these hold for perfections of Schubert varieties, and étale cohomology does not see perfection. So the gap is very likely fillable, but it is not filled in the paper. Zhu presents §2.4.4–2.4.5 as a sketch ('We sketch it here and refer to loc. cit. for details').

review.reason: The quotations match the images of pp. 453–454. The trace formula is the only link from Theorem 2.35 (a statement about Hecke algebras) to Lemma 2.34, and through Lemmas 2.30 and 2.29 (p. 450) to Proposition 2.21 and the symmetric monoidal structure in Theorem 0.3. I checked the sources. LV12 (arXiv 1109.4606) proves the trace interpretation (§3, via B×B over F_p-bar, a Frobenius twisted by the swap, and [KL] purity) only for finite Weyl groups. §7.1–7.2 say only that the ⋄-twisted and affine versions hold 'with essentially the same proof' over k((ε)). LY13 (published §3.1) call their affine version 'an elaboration of this remark' and state (3.2), (3.5) and the §7.4 formula (through (7.1)) without detailed proof. Zhu needs a new setting: the perfect Witt-vector affine flag variety, with ⋄ = Ad(ω)∘*. His involution Ψ_μ is defined through Gr^op, N_μ and Corollary 2.26, because θ maps Gr to Gr^op and there is no loop-group sheaf theory (Remark 2.25). Relating it to the τ^*-involution of a Lusztig–Vogan realization requires an Iwahori-level analogue of Lemma 2.24 and Corollary 2.26 and compatibility with pullback along Fl → Gr. The paper supplies none of this, only 'similar interpretations were given ... Such interpretations in particular imply'. The preceding 'The usual Kazhdan–Lusztig theory ... works in our situation' is likewise only asserted. Case for the defence: the LV argument is formal (sheaf–function dictionary, purity and parity, rank-one computations), étale cohomology does not see perfection, and the gap is very likely fillable. It is still a load-bearing step asserted without proof, so 'gap' with reach 'the proof' is right; no stated result is shown false. One small inaccuracy in the first reading's reason: the explicit 'We sketch it here and refer to loc. cit. for details' is on p. 452 and concerns Lemma 2.34 ⇒ Lemma 2.30. It does not label §2.4.5 as a sketch.

The relative Frobenius is X -> X x_{Y,σ_Y} Y, x ↦ (σ_X(x), f(x)), and its target is X x_{Y,σ_Y} Y, so it cannot be base-changed along a map to Y. The cover that works is U x_{Y,σ_Y} Y -> X x_{Y,σ_Y} Y, the base change of the étale cover U -> X, so it is itself an étale cover. review.reason: The quotation is verbatim on the p. 467 image. Lemma A.7 is stated for arbitrary algebraic spaces over k, which may be non-reduced, and then A -> A^{p^-∞} and B -> B^{p^-∞} need not be injective. 'All coefficients of h are in A' can then only mean 'in the image of A', and h(b) = g(b)^{p^n} = 0 holds only in B^{p^-∞}. For a lift h̃ ∈ A[x], h̃(b) lies in ker(B -> B^{p^-∞}), which consists of the elements killed by some power of Frobenius, and need not be 0. The repair is short and correct: h̃(b)^{p^m} = 0, so b is a root of the monic polynomial h̃(x)^{p^m} ∈ A[x]. The lemma is true. So this is a gap, as the first reading says. But a gap means the written proof of (7) (direction 'f^{p^-∞} integral ⇒ f integral') is incomplete in the non-reduced case, so the reach is 'the proof', not 'nothing'. The applications of A.7(7) (Theorem A.30, Prop. A.32) use only the easy direction.

review.reason: The quotation is verbatim on the p. 482 image. The mathematics is right. In characteristic p, unipotent groups need not be connected: the constant group Z/p ⊂ G_a is unipotent. So the condition admits disconnected J_1, and the independence claim then fails. Take J = Z/p, X = Spec k (k algebraically closed). Both J_1 = J and J_1' = {1} satisfy every stated condition, but P_{J/J}(X) = Vect while P_{J/{1}}(X) = Rep_{Q̄_ℓ}(Z/p), with p simple objects. The latter also agrees with the first-paragraph definition of P_J for pfp J, while the former does not. Connectedness of J alone does not rescue it either: G_a^{p^-∞} acting on X = G_a^{p^-∞} through the Artin-Schreier map has kernel J_1 = Z/p, and P_J(X) = Rep(Z/p) ≠ Vect = P_{J/J_1}(X). Classification: the defect is the omission of the word 'connected'. The sentence justifies independence 'By (A.3.4)', and (A.3.4) is stated only for connected J_1. Every J_1 the paper actually uses is a connected congruence subgroup L^+G^{(h)} = ker(L^+G -> L^hG) (§2.1.1, p. 429). So the intended hypothesis is fixed by the cited result and by every use, and with it the claim is true. This matches how missing hypotheses clear from context are classified elsewhere in this verification (misprint, affects nothing). 'Error' with 'affects nothing' is not coherent here: if the independence claim were counted as a genuine false assertion, it would affect a stated claim. The cohomology half ((A.3.6)) needs only unipotence. For two connected choices it gives the same answer as for the categories.

diagnostics.name: Noncommuting Witt chart factorization
diagnostics.result: Five odd primes: X=Ag recovers integral g by A⁻¹X; XA⁻¹ contains −1/p². The displayed integral matrices have X0=[[-1,−1],[0,0]] and X1=[[1,0],[1,1]], satisfying the relevant first-coordinate open condition.

diagnostics.name: Determinant-normalizing unit
diagnostics.result: For four primes and every nonzero residue unit, λ detX=p² forces detX=p² λ⁻¹ modulo p³; p=5,u=2 rejects the printed inverse convention.

diagnostics.name: Additive Koszul parity
diagnostics.result: All four parity pairs checked; the printed multiplicative-sign exponent gives −1 even at the unit, whereas ε_A ε_B gives the correct unit and odd/odd signs.

diagnostics.name: IC and weight degree shifts
diagnostics.result: For dimensions0–9 and21 weight degrees, C=IC[−d] restricts in degree0 and H_c^w(IC) has unshifted degree w+d. The smooth-curve IC[1] and dualizing[2](1) are distinct.

diagnostics.name: Involution trace forces scalar
diagnostics.result: 66 eigenvalue-multiplicity cases verify that an involution with trace ±dimension has only that sign as eigenvalue. The characteristic-zero diagonalization theorem remains a proof obligation.

diagnostics.name: Minuscule inverse and Hodge frame
diagnostics.result: At three primes, β=p makes β⁻¹(p) integral and (1/p)β⁻¹(p) nonintegral. For b=diag(1,p), V=diag(p,1) has mod-p image e2, distinct from the fixed μ(t)=diag(t,1) weight-one line.

diagnostics.name: Torus nonemptiness
diagnostics.result: 49 valuation/coweight pairs: the torus ADLV condition is v(b)=μ. Since rho and defect vanish, the unqualified dimension formula would assign zero even to every mismatched empty space.

diagnostics.name: Isogeny-chain indexing and rank
diagnostics.result: Tower ranges0≤i<h include the initial step and stop at h for eight h values. Forty rank cases distinguish full Dieudonné rank2hn from one τ-component rank n.

diagnostics.name: Ordered norm telescoping
diagnostics.result: 81 pairs of unipotent frame changes verify the two-factor norm telescoping law with identity coefficient automorphism. This is an order diagnostic, not a proof of the Frobenius-semilinear theorem.

diagnostics.name: Top trace counterexamples
diagnostics.result: The geometric component count of Spec F_(q²) is two. Constant and degree2/3/5 maps of P1 have top pullback multipliers0/2/3/5, refuting the asserted arbitrary-morphism trace identity; the geometric pullback-degree theorem is a separate imported proof.
